title: Season 2 skepticism, parent opinions vs. good results, & Tarot cards for teachers
author: Alexander Russo
summary: This is Alexander Russo's Weekend Recap for The Grade, his newsletter on education journalism, combined with an unlocked section on who decides what makes a good school. The recap notes expert advice on responsible school shooting coverage, SF Chronicle reporter Jill Tucker's criticism of the explicit instruction ideas in Season 2 of Sold a Story, and a former urban educator's account of adults complicit in a culture of failure. The unlocked section revisits the Nice White Parents framing through a Seattle parent's complaint that it collapsed accountability for parents who advocate for their kids. Russo then argues that some journalists mistake parents' immediate survey preferences for evidence of school quality, warning that a school can poll well and still be a poor place to learn. It closes with two reporting insights and a clip of Emily Hanford describing how she moved from antipathy toward explicit instruction to accepting the evidence.
points: Russo argues that parent poll responses should not outweigh measures of students' academic experience and long-term need for skills and knowledge.
He warns that casting doubt on external metrics muddies the water and lets a school look good on preferences alone.
Journalist Jill Tucker's criticism of Season 2 of Sold a Story shows that the explicit-instruction debate is still contested in education media.
The Nice White Parents framing is questioned for treating parent advocacy as suspect and diluting accountability.
Emily Hanford's recounted shift from disliking explicit instruction to following the evidence is offered as a model of journalistic open-mindedness.
